tagline.text: A fortress-like World Heritage church atop an 85-step hill

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–1,500 per person (half day from Vigan)

image.credit: Philip Nalangan / CC BY 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: An 18th-century brick church on a hill south of Vigan, one of the UNESCO World Heritage "Baroque Churches of the Philippines" alongside the churches of Paoay, Miagao, and San Agustin. Climb 85 stone steps to reach its massive buttresses and octagonal bell tower, as imposing as a fortress.
The full name of Santa Maria Church is "Nuestra Señora de la Asunción" (Our Lady of the Assumption). It stands atop a hill rising from the center of the town of Santa Maria in Ilocos Sur, about
40km

south of Vigan. Looking up from the coastal road, the red-brick church and bell tower seem to wrap around the whole hill, looking less like a church than a walled fortress. This distinctive setting is what earned it a place, in
, on the UNESCO World Heritage list as one of the "Baroque Churches of the Philippines," alongside San Agustin Church in Manila, Paoay Church in Ilocos Norte, and Miagao Church in Iloilo.
Santa Maria began in
as a small mission station attached to the neighboring parish of Narvacan, and the current church was begun by the Augustinians in
. The freestanding four-story octagonal bell tower beside the church was built in

. According to legend, a statue of the Virgin Mary kept elsewhere kept disappearing, only to be found again and again in a guava tree on this hill, so a church was eventually built on the spot. That statue, affectionately called "Apo Baket" (grandmother) by locals, still stands on the altar today.
The church is built of brick and stone in the classic "Earthquake Baroque" style. Rows of massive square buttresses line both side walls to withstand earthquakes, and the long nave, about
in length, stretches along the ridge of the hill. The Philippine government designated it a National Historical Landmark in
and a National Cultural Treasure in
, and in
Pope Francis elevated the church to the status of Minor Basilica.

The church itself can be seen in an hour or two, making it an easy half-day trip from Vigan, or a good stop on the way between Manila and Vigan. Quieter than the more crowded Paoay and Vigan, it's especially worth recommending to history, architecture, and photography enthusiasts who want to take in the texture of old brick and the marks of time at an unhurried pace.

The granite staircase leading from the town road up to the church is Santa Maria's signature feature. Both the view looking up at the church and bell tower from the bottom of the steps, and the view of the town looking down from the top, are worth photographing.

Thick square buttresses line both sides of the church, offering the clearest look at the hallmarks of Earthquake Baroque architecture. Walk slowly along the wall and take in the texture of the brick and lime mortar.

The freestanding four-story octagonal bell tower, set apart from the main church, is said to have been built separately so that if it collapsed in an earthquake, it wouldn't fall onto the church itself. Morning, when the red brick tower stands out against a blue sky, is the best time to photograph it.

blocks.title: Inside the Church of Our Lady of the Assumption

children.text: The "Apo Baket" statue of the Virgin Mary is enshrined at the altar, at the end of the long, unadorned nave. What impresses here isn't ornate decoration but the quiet created by thick walls and a high ceiling.

blocks.title: The old cemetery and chapel ruins

children.text: On the hill behind the church, an old cemetery enclosed by a brick wall and the ruins of a collapsed funerary chapel (camposanto) still remain. Among the grass-covered ruins, you can feel the weight of past time.
A leading waterfall in Ilocos Sur, about
20–30 minutes
inland from town by car — a good pairing with the church for a half-day trip.

blocks.title: Attending the Feast of the Assumption

children.text: Every year on
August 15
, the Feast of the Assumption, a grand Mass and procession fill the town of Santa Maria with a festive atmosphere.
Board a southbound bus or van at the Vigan bus terminal
Arrive in the town of Santa Maria, head to the foot of the church steps by tricycle or on foot
Climb the 85 stone steps, taking photos of the church and bell tower
Visit the church interior, then walk the buttressed side walls and bell tower
Stroll the old cemetery and chapel ruins behind the church
Charter a tricycle for a side trip to Pinsal Falls (optional)
Lunch in town, then return to Vigan or continue toward La Union

If you're traveling from Manila to Vigan, it also works well to take the Vigan-bound bus and get off first in Santa Maria to see the church, then catch the next northbound bus on to Vigan. Ask in advance whether a shop at the foot of the church or a tricycle driver can hold your larger luggage.
Partas, Dominion, and other buses bound for Vigan and Laoag, departing from Cubao, Pasay, and Sampaloc in Manila, pass through Santa Maria. The trip takes about
7–9 hours
, for a one-way fare of about
. Let the driver know in advance that you're getting off near Santa Maria Church.
From Vigan, a southbound bus or van (toward Candon or San Fernando) takes about
1 hour
, for a fare of about
The nearest airport is Laoag International Airport (LAO), about
1 hour 10 minutes
from Manila. From the airport to Santa Maria is about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours
by car, and it's usually combined into an itinerary that passes through Vigan on the way down.
Taking NLEX–SCTEX–TPLEX and then the La Union coastal road (MacArthur Highway) north takes about
6–8 hours
from Manila. There's space to park at the foot of the church steps and on the hill above, but it fills quickly on feast days.
The church sits in the center of town, so you can walk from where the bus drops you or take a tricycle (about
). If you're also visiting Pinsal Falls, it's more convenient to charter a round-trip tricycle (about
The Ilocos region's dry season,
November–May
, is the best time to visit. The sharp contrast between blue sky and red brick makes for great photos, and the stairs and hillside paths stay dry and safe underfoot.
December–February
is relatively cool, but in
March–May
, midday temperatures climb to around
, making the shade-poor steps and courtyard quite hot. Visit early in the morning or late in the afternoon.
June–October

is the rainy season, affected by the southwest monsoon and typhoons, when the stone steps and old cemetery paths can turn slippery and traffic on the coastal road may be delayed. During Holy Week, the church fills with pilgrims making the rounds of multiple churches in "Visita Iglesia," and around the Feast of the Assumption on
August 15
, festival events bring the town to life.

The town of Santa Maria has few traveler-oriented accommodations, so most visitors stay in Vigan, about an hour away by car, and visit from there. Heritage hotels converted from old mansions in Vigan's old town run about
a night, and guesthouses about
. If you're continuing south, a simple hotel in downtown Candon (about
) is another option.

The town has small Filipino eateries (carinderias) and bakeries where you can grab a simple meal. Try Ilocos Sur's signature dishes — crispy fried pork bagnet, the vegetable stew pinakbet, and Vigan longganisa — and save a proper sit-down meal for Vigan, where you can pair it with the orange, rice-flour-crusted empanada. To the south, Candon is famous for kalamay, a sweet rice cake made with glutinous rice and coconut, a popular souvenir.
The best time to photograph the church's facade and bell tower is
, when the morning sun from the east brings out the brick's color most vividly.
The two most popular shots are looking up at the whole church from the foot of the steps, and an angled shot along the buttresses of the side wall.
Pause your visit during Mass, and if a wedding or funeral Mass is underway, wait quietly outside.
Remove your hat before entering the church, and avoid sleeveless tops and short shorts.
Pairing this with Paoay Church lets you compare two Earthquake Baroque churches from the same World Heritage listing.
Restaurants and tricycles in town take cash only, so bring small bills.
Follow your location on a map app so you don't miss your stop on the bus — the church is close once you start seeing the hill from the road.

This church is a World Heritage Site more than 200 years old. Climbing on the walls or buttresses, or scratching or writing on the brick, is strictly forbidden and can be punished as damage to cultural heritage.
The stone steps are uneven in height and become slippery in the rain. If traveling with elderly or less mobile companions, climb slowly with breaks, or consider driving up to the hilltop instead.
With little shade in the courtyard and on the steps, heatstroke is a real risk at midday in
March–May
. Bring water and a hat.
The old cemetery and chapel ruins behind the church have walls that could collapse, so don't go inside them.
Large buses and trucks move fast along the coastal road. Be especially careful getting off the bus and crossing the street.
During typhoon season, the coastal road linking Vigan and La Union may be cut off or buses delayed.
